newsitem.title: FRANCE: Publicis forms joint TV programme venture.
newsitem.headline: Publicis forms joint TV programme venture.

text.p: French advertising group Publicis is creating a joint venture with a prominent French television presenter to produce television programmes financed by advertisers, a senior Publicis executive said on Tuesday.
Daniel Saada, chairman of Publicis' sponsoring unit TV Mission, said Publicis was following the demand of its clients in moving into programme production.
The venture, Etoile TV, will be owned 51 percent by Publicis and 49 percent by Coyote Conseil, the production house of television presenter Christophe Dechavanne, he said.
"It is the job of a group like Publicis to be in advance of the expectations of its clients," Saada said, adding that Etoile TV would "allow advertisers to have a means of expression".
He said Etoile TV was the first venture of its kind in France.

Publicis was going further than an existing partnership between Havas's Euro RSCG and the production company of television presenter Arthur, by creating a joint company with the production house, he said.
Saada declined to say how much would be invested in the joint venture, but said for Publicis it was primarily a human investment.
He expected programmes pre-sold to television channels to be ready by around the end of this year.
Etoile TV will focus on magazine, social and entertainment-style programmes where Dechavanne is best known and where Coyote has expertise, Saada said.
In the U.S. sitcoms have been financed by advertisers, but Saada said Etoile TV could tackle that type of programme later.
Initially it would attack the French market, but would aim to benefit from Publicis's European network to export programmes to other European countries, he said.
France has five open-access terrestrial channels and one encoded pay television channel, but cable and satellite services which carry thematic channels are relatively recent.
Saada did not see Etoile TV restricting itself to the better-established terrestrial channels.
Thematic channels have an "audience quality" which could interest advertisers, he said.
He said the viewer might have no clue that the programme was financed by an advertiser, if the advertiser chose not to announc this and not to have any advertising break showing its products.
The format would depend on the advertiser and the channel buying the programme, he said. -- Sue Landau, Paris newsroom, 33 1 4221 5452
